summary: Forecasting experts hold divergent but generally moderate views on whether a political protest with at least 600,000 participants (measured by the French Ministry of the Interior) will occur in France before January 1, 2026. Throughout their analyses, experts recognize France’s rich tradition of large-scale protest, especially in response to austerity measures and governmental crises; recent events (September 2025) saw over 500,000 participants but turnout has since declined. Several major factors are at play: (1) the persistent political instability, unpopular austerity, and historic capacity of unions to mobilize suggest an elevated risk if a new trigger event (such as forced budget passage, use of Article 49.3, or a harsh repression incident) arises; (2) the downward momentum in turnout, protest fatigue, lack of scheduled future mass mobilization, and potential for government concessions work against another mass action exceeding the threshold; (3) the official reliance on Interior Ministry count, which tends to be conservative, makes the bar harder to clear, even when union numbers are higher. Experts differ in their quantitative estimates, with probabilities ranging from 30–68%. The more optimistic forecasters (Political Science: Resource Mobilization Theory, Sociology: Social Movement Theory, French Studies) highlight the acute unresolved crisis and potential for a trigger event, judging chances moderately to substantially above even odds (58–68%). Others (OSINT, Political Science: Contentious Politics, POS, Collective Action Theory) lean below 50%, emphasizing declining momentum and seasonal effects, but note that a sharp political escalation could still quickly change the protest dynamic. Consensus emphasizes that—barring a new, highly provocative government move or crisis—current trends point to no further protest exceeding the threshold, though all agree that volatile conditions and the French protest tradition mean a risk of sudden remobilization persists.
